item.title: Send the Firefighters to the Fires
item.description: Send the firefighters to the firesEnterprise software keeps forgetting a century of good advice about what deserves our attention.House fire in New Zealand neighborhoodIf a user’s job is to fix what’s broken, the screen should show what’s broken first. Sounds pretty obvious. It’s also not new. Frederick Taylor argued for it in 1903. Xerox PARC designed for it in the ’90s. Industrial control rooms wrote it into a standard. Yet enterprise software keeps forgetting this.Imagine a fire department that dispatches trucks in the order houses were built. Or by date last renovated. Every house gets a visit eventually, and some of them happen to be on fire. That’s pretty absurd, right? Yet I’ve seen the equivalent more times than I care to remember.A lot of enterprise work boils down to one job: here’s a collection of things, some of them have problems, go fix the problems. Devices out of compliance. Certificates about to expire. Invoices that failed to reconcile. Tickets breaching SLA. The KPI is simply “issues resolved.”The UI has one job: get the user to the fires and hand them the hose.So how did we forget? Not because the ideas are hard. Enterprise software just has a habit of designing for everyone except the person actually using it. It’s designing for the buyer in the demo, for the team racing to ship, for the data model that sorts things for free. None of them pay for it. But the user does, every shift, one scroll at a time.Start with the jobClayton Christensen had a simple idea: people don’t buy products for their features. They hire them to get a job done. It’s now known as Jobs to Be Done, or JTBD (Christensen et al., 2016; open-access overview). In enterprise triage, the job is about as plain as it gets: fix what’s broken. Finding it should be the product’s job.So why do so many screens ignore this? Here’s the pattern I see over and over again. A screen lists 400 objects, and twelve need attention. They’re scattered somewhere between page 3 and page 17. It’s Where’s Waldo, except Waldo is a production outage.Sometimes there’s a status column. Maybe a small red pill, sitting politely in column six of a list sorted by anything but what matters. A human can work out which items are broken. But the interface is acting obtuse and unhelpful.Consider the following twenty services. I’ll keep coming back to them.Before: 20 rows, sorted by last updated, every column visibleA service table with 20 rows, sorted by last updated. Its Health and Tier columns are listed separately, so the most urgent services are hard to spot. For example, payments-gw is failing and Tier 1 but appears near the bottom.After: focus on the firesService alerts by severity: 2 critical (payments-gw, billing-db) and 4 warnings (search-index, mail-relay, audit-log, cache-02), each with a cause. 14 services are passing checks.In the first table, the two critical services sit in rows sixteen and nineteen, and nothing calls them critical. You have to cross-reference Health and Tier yourself: search-index is only Degraded, but it’s Tier 1; mail-relay is Failing, but it’s Tier 3. Meanwhile, Uptime reads 99.92% for payments-gw, which is failing right now. The fires-first view does that math for you. Same data, different job.Now imagine hearing that table instead. If the headers are marked up properly, a screen reader announces which column you’re in as you move through it (W3C, F91). So a screen reader user can walk down the Health column one cell at a time. That’s still twenty announcements to find six problems, plus a hop to the Tier column for each one. And that’s the best case: many enterprise data grids are built from divs, virtualized, or paginated, and those shortcuts break. Many enterprises don’t hire people who can build accessible tables (Brad Frost calls them front-of-the-front-end developers), but that’s another story. For every column of noise we leave in, someone has to sit through it.None of this is malicious. Nobody in the review said “hey, let’s bury the critical issues!” The order happened by default, because nobody dug into the JTBD.The table as a design cop-outBad sort order is an outcome of enterprise’s unfortunate love affair with the table as a magic bullet.The reasoning goes: we don’t know exactly what users want, so let’s give them all the data and let them search, filter, and sort. It sounds like giving users control. In reality, it’s an abdication.Those are tools for exploring and hunting: browsing to see what’s there, or tracking down something you know exists. But when they become the main interface for task work, the product team has handed its job to the user. Every session, someone sorts by health, scrolls past the Passing rows, cross-checks the tier, and finds payments-gw. Again. Multiply that by every user, every day. That’s triage the product could have done once.At some point, some smarty-pants will suggest saved filters: let users build and save their own “To-dos” view (health is failing, sorted by tier). Problem solved, right? Not quite! That’s a workaround stacked on the cop-out. Users end up designing the default screen for you because you shipped the wrong one.Asking the hard questions is usually right and rarely rewarded.Why smart teams keep doing thisTo be fair, the people shipping these screens aren’t careless. The forces pushing them toward the table are real, and a lot of them trace back to one thing: in sales-led enterprise software, the buyer isn’t the user.Jason Lemkin said it bluntly back in 2012: “you, the end user, aren’t the customer for most true enterprise software” (Lemkin, SaaStr). A year later, Martin Eriksson made the same distinction for product managers: “the user and the purchaser are different people with different needs” (Eriksson, Mind the Product).The buyer’s worst case is a boring demo. The user’s worst case is an outage with their name on it. Guess who the screen gets designed for. Not every lazy sort comes from sales, but a sales-led motion makes lazy sorts easier to ship and harder to undo.Defaults feel safe. Every record has a created_at and an updated_at, so sorting by them is free. “Severity” doesn’t exist until someone designs it. Meanwhile, stakeholders worry that if healthy items aren’t visible, users will assume they’re missing, and on an RFP checklist, a hidden column might as well not exist. So everything stays on screen.Nobody talks to each other. Taiichi Ohno’s 5 Whys only works if you can reach the person with the answer. In enterprise, there are too many layers between the people willing to ask and the people able to answer. The only two people reliably talking are the salesperson and the buyer. The salesperson is paid for the close, and asking why five times only gets in the way. Conway’s law predicts the result: systems mirror how their makers communicate. A neutral sort is what that silence looks like on screen.“Ask ‘why’ five times about every matter.” — Taiichi Ohno, ToyotaDashboards are built for the demo. People love dashboards that look like command centers in movies. Walls of screens! Scrolling numbers! Blinking maps! Stephen Few was criticizing exactly this two decades ago, arguing that dashboards should support real-time situation awareness for decision making, not impress the room (Few, 2007; Information Dashboard Design, 2006). Density still wins sales calls, which is the sales motion showing up in the UI. Developers and PMs love it too: every widget and column is a feature someone built.Tables are cheap and familiar. Every component library ships one, and every IC has built a dozen, so it’s what everyone reaches for first. Inline editing is one prop away, so someone will eventually float turning every cell into a form field. Cheap to build, expensive to use.Tables become the anti-pattern of choice when user needs are poorly understood, search capabilities are inadequate, and managing complexity is an afterthought.Notice what these have in common? Each one optimizes for the team’s comfort or the buyer’s first impression, not the user’s job. The table can never be wrong, because it never commits to anything.Tables aren’t the enemyTo be clear, I’m not anti-table. Reporting, analysis, and bulk admin are table work. User questions can change week to week, and pinning them down takes the kind of conversations we’ve already seen are rare. Designing for that is tough, so a flexible table is an honest answer.The line I draw is this: open-ended questions need flexible tables. Known jobs need opinionated ones.Yet sometimes the best table is the one you don’t build! Think about what people actually do with a big table, and where that work belongs:Slice and pivot? Let them export to (or integrate with) the BI tools they already know.Report up to leadership? Send a scheduled summary, not a screenshot of 400 rows.Reconcile against another system? That’s an integration or an API. Please don’t subject a human being to comparing two systems row by row.Hand evidence to auditors? Send an export instead of buying them a seat, which only gets them a login they’ll barely use, to a worse BI tool.Excel, Tableau, and Power BI are established, they’re good at analysis, and your users already know them. Your product doesn’t need to compete. Just keep the fires list live and in-app.So the question isn’t table or no table. It’s what goes in it, and in what order. If you can write the user’s job in one sentence, and “resolve the issues” is that sentence, you know enough to decide: fires first, ranked by severity, healthy rows summarized. A table sorted by last updated with every row at equal weight is just an inventory. It tells users what exists, not what needs their attention.Management by exception, a century laterOne of my core design principles fits in four words: no news is good news. I didn’t invent it. In 1903, Frederick Taylor called it the exception principle: a manager shouldn’t be swamped with every report, only with what deviates from the standard (Taylor, Shop Management).“The manager should receive only condensed, summarized, and invariably comparative reports.” — Frederick Winslow Taylor, Shop Management (1903)Swap “manager” for “user” and it’s a design brief. There’s no reason to emphasize what’s working. Working is the expected state; it’s what the customer pays for. But there’s every reason to emphasize what isn’t, because that’s the only part that needs a human.Every pixel that gives a healthy object the same weight as a broken one is friction against the KPI. If the metric is issues resolved, a screen that hides issues isn’t neutral. It’s working against the business. And noise isn’t just visual. For a screen reader user, it’s time.So design as if the user’s job performance depends on your decisions. Because it does! When issues slip through the cracks, nobody blames the designer who picked the default sort. They blame the user who didn’t spot payments-gw in time. They inherit our defaults, our clutter, and our shallow thinking, and they’re the ones who get penalized for it.That’s the bar. It’s not “does it follow the design system” or “did stakeholders sign off.” It’s “does this make the person using it better at their job?”What control rooms already knowIronically, real control rooms don’t look like the movies. In refineries and power plants, operator screens are guided by the ISA-101 standard for industrial interfaces (ISA, 2015), which builds on the high-performance HMI work of Bill Hollifield and colleagues (The High Performance HMI Handbook). Normal operation stays gray and calm. Color is saved for when something’s wrong.https://medium.com/media/3a2b27bedfc398539b462d0027464e6c/hrefThe unsexy truth is that sometimes, that’s all a dashboard needs to be: a prioritized list of what’s on fire and the means to put it out, not a bunch of widgets fighting for the user’s attention. Many may not like it, but that’s what peak performance looks like. Operators knew it long before enterprise SaaS did.Silence has to be earnedHere’s a fair objection: users need reassurance. If I only show problems, how does anybody know the rest is fine?Sure, Jakob Nielsen’s first usability heuristic covers it. Systems should keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within reasonable time (Harley, NN/g). No news is only good news if the silence is trustworthy. An empty screen could mean everything is healthy, or that the sync broke an hour ago. If users can’t tell the difference, they’ll go back to scanning the full table.So design the quiet state as deliberately as the loud one. Don’t list the healthy items. Summarize them with confidence.Empty screen: healthy, or broken?Earned silenceJust a count, a timestamp, and a way to dig deeper. You’re still reporting the good news. You’re just not giving it top billing.Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown described this balance in 1995 as calm technology: information that sits in the periphery of our attention and moves to the center only when it matters (Weiser and Brown, 1995). In their words, the periphery is “informing without overburdening.” That’s the quiet state. It gives users permission to stop looking. Giving users their time back might be the most underrated thing an enterprise tool can offer.What fires-first actually looks likeA fires-first approach isn’t just the same table with a different sort. Here’s what separates it, with credit where it’s due.Severity, not just status. A small fire next to a gas station beats a big one in an empty lot. An expired certificate on payments-gw outranks one on a test server, even if both say “Failing.” Health tells you what broke. Tier tells you how much it matters. Severity needs both. Remember that severity doesn’t exist until someone designs it? This is what designing it looks like.Urgency and importance are separate axes. The idea is usually traced to a 1954 Eisenhower speech, and Stephen Covey, A. Roger Merrill, and Rebecca Merrill turned it into four quadrants in First Things First (Hoang, Rework). Plot issues on that matrix, and users can make meaningful choices about what to fix now, schedule, delegate, or snooze.Lead straight into investigation. Fires seldom have a one-click fix. The real job is usually figuring out what went wrong, so each item should invite investigation.Notify, so nobody has to watch. People have better things to do than babysit your app. When payments-gw catches fire, tell the person who can fix it, wherever they already work: email, Slack, Teams. The fires list is where they go to act, not where they sit and wait.Restraint on alerts. Healthcare has studied the opposite failure for years. When clinicians are flooded with warnings, they become desensitized and start overriding the critical ones along with the trivial ones (AHRQ PSNet, “Alert Fatigue”). If 300 of 400 items say “Warning,” your users will do the same. A severity model that can’t say “this doesn’t matter now” isn’t a severity model.Let users snooze. Some fires can’t be fought today: a vendor hasn’t replied, or the fix needs a maintenance window. Snoozing dials down the noise without pretending the issue is solved, and it comes back on schedule.Resolution is visible. When a fire goes out, it leaves the list and the count drops. That feedback loop makes the KPI real to the person doing the work.Everything is still one click away. The full table, healthy rows included, for the audit, the export, and the curious.Health sets urgency, and Tier sets importance. Only payments-gw and billing-db land in Fix now.“I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important.” — Dwight D. Eisenhower, quoting J. Roscoe Miller, 1954The top-right quadrant leads the fires list. Everything else still has a home.Not sure where to start? Watch how users triage today: what they sort by, what they scroll past, what they export. Your users have already mentally drafted the spec.Dispatch, not censusA census counts everyone equally. That’s its job. A dispatch center decides who needs help first and sends people there.Most enterprise dashboards are built like a census: complete, neutral, accurate. And no help to someone whose job is putting out the fires.Taylor got there in 1903. Weiser and Brown in 1995. Few in 2006. The ISA-101 committee in 2015. Same direction, a century apart. The knowledge isn’t missing. What’s missing is defining what “on fire” means, ranking it, designing the quiet state, and wiring up the notifications.Do the extra work so your users don’t have to. That’s the job.Further readingIn order of appearance:Clayton M. Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon, and David S. item.title: If AI works from anywhere, why are we commuting to watch it?
item.description: The collaboration they promised, in practice.Companies say it’s about collaboration. That’s garbage. The reality is a room full of people in headphones, doing alone what they could’ve done at home.The recent post from Alexa von Tobel on LinkedIn.Alexa von Tobel, who runs an early-stage fund and has backed a long list of founders, posted a small, honest question. She hadn’t been pitched a single remote-only company in six months, and she wanted to know if anyone else was seeing it.The replies were a mix. A few pushed back. One said she had landed a remote role just fine and that nobody had to pitch her anything. Another figured the remote crowd was mostly off building their own companies now.The reply that stuck with me came from a CEO, who said being fully remote would be harder, and less fun. It resonated because he is half right. Something real does get lost when everyone is scattered. He is just wrong about what fixes it.What I haven’t seen is anyone ask what should be the obvious question. If the office is winning, what exactly is it “winning” people back to do?This matters more than it used to, because the thing we always said the office was for has left the building (pun intended). We told ourselves we showed up every day to get the work done together. The making, the producing, the actual output. You went to the office because that was where the work physically got made, and it got made faster with everyone in one place.Thomas Allen measured the reason decades ago at MIT. The closer two people sit, the more they actually talk, and past about fifty feet the conversation falls off a cliff.Proximity was the whole point. The commute bought you that.The work doesn’t live there anymore. It runs on its own now, in the cloud, whether you are at your desk or asleep. Gartner expects forty percent of business software to have agents built into it by the end of 2026, up from under five percent a year earlier.Offices may still exist, but perhaps we lost the reason for them.My position is simple, even if the fight over it refuses to be. The office isn’t dead, but it shouldn’t be mandatory. It’s worth protecting for the handful of things people can only do well together, the ones AI can’t touch. Instead it’s being forced on everyone for the work that no longer needs a building at all.The production work is moving into the software itself, fast.The work left the buildingThe founders von Tobel is funding are increasingly building agents that do the production themselves. Y Combinator’s recent cohorts are full of companies whose entire pitch is autonomous software that writes, tests, and ships code with a human barely touching it, and the firm’s own partners say AI has collapsed the cost of producing software by a factor of ten to a hundred.This is not a forecast. It already shows up in who has a job. Erik Brynjolfsson and his colleagues at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab tracked real payroll data and found that employment for workers aged twenty-two to twenty-five in the most AI-exposed jobs sits about nineteen percent below where it should be, while their older colleagues are fine.The gap is coming from companies not hiring junior team members, because AI is doing the checkable, process-heavy tasks that used to justify an entry-level seat. You know, the production work, the stuff we all started our careers doing.It is not only software. Anthropic, looking at how its own models actually get used, found that coding is the single biggest category, and that while most use still has AI working alongside a person, a large and growing share, more than four in ten interactions, is now the model doing the task outright rather than assisting.The line between the two is blurry, but it is clearly moving in one direction.Designers feel it and say so. Francisco Barrera Aros points out that AI has swallowed the how of building an interface and is coming for the what, which is why job boards have started sprouting roles like AI Product Designer that nobody could have described two years ago.AI took over the task of doing the work. The deciding, however, is still yours, and the deciding is where the money is.Let’s look at what that leaves for the purpose of an office. For a century it was where the production happened, because production needed people in one spot with the files, the tools, and each other. Take that out, hand it to the agents, and the physical building becomes a very expensive room you commute to in order to do work that could happen anywhere.Which should, by any reasonable prediction, empty the place out.We all remember 2020, right? The pandemic sent nearly everyone home at once. Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom, and Steven Davis called it a mass social experiment in working from home, with Americans doing roughly half of all paid hours from home through most of 2020, up from about five percent before.The floors we were told could never go dark went dark, and the striking part, in their data, is how many people were surprised they could do the job from home at all. The mandates coming down treat remote work as an unproven indulgence, when we have years of evidence that most of the job travels. The question should be which parts don’t work and why not?The work got portable, and the founders packed into one city anyway.So everyone scattered, right?Obviously, work is more portable than it has ever been, but the freer people are to work anywhere, the more they actually want to be together.Y Combinator, which has funded a good chunk of the companies building these agents, spent years running its batches remotely, and in those years its founders were scattered all over the map. Then it brought the program back in person, in San Francisco, and the founders came right back with it. The trend is easy to see in YC’s own public directory, which one analysis tracked batch by batch.When the program went remote, barely a quarter of companies listed San Francisco as home. Once it came back in person, that climbed past three quarters, and a chunk of those founders kept choosing the city even after the three months ended and nothing required them to stay. The same batches are stuffed with startups whose product is autonomous software.The people automating the production hardest are also the people most determined to sit in the same zip code while they do it.This is one contender to define whole AI era, at least for the workforce. Gensler’s global survey found that the workers most embedded in AI are also the most collaborative and the most drawn to the office, which is the reverse of the lonely-robot future everyone predicted.As AI takes more of the solo production, the human collaboration it can’t do becomes a scarce, valuable thing, and the people who live in these tools feel the pull toward the room where that still happens.If the office were really about the work, this is backwards. These founders have built, and are selling, the exact tools that make location irrelevant. They could run these companies from anywhere, and they tell you so with a straight face in the pitch deck. Then they sign a lease three blocks from each other.The clustering is telling you something that a pitch deck won’t. Whatever they are gathering for, it is not the production, because they already shipped the production to the cloud. It is the other thing.There is real research on what that other thing is. Daniel Carmody, Martina Mazzarello, Paolo Santi and their colleagues at MIT’s Senseable City Lab studied what happened to people’s networks when everyone went remote, and found that distance measurably starved the weak ties, the loose connections that only form when people share a space. Weak ties are the people you don’t work with closely, the person two teams over, the one you only ever talk to because you both happened to be refilling coffee.Mark Granovetter named their importance decades ago, in the work that gave us the phrase. The loose connections, not the close ones, are where new information and unlikely ideas actually travel. They are also the first thing to die when everyone is a tile on a screen, because nobody schedules a video call with the person two teams over for no reason.That is what the founders are re-clustering to get back. Not the work. The accidental stuff around the work. The collisions you cannot put on a calendar, which turn out to be the one thing the agents can’t do for you and the screen can’t give you either.Forcing people together in an open plan cut face-to-face interaction by about seventy percent.The office we actually builtStroll into a lot of these offices and look at what is actually happening.Rows of people who commuted in to sit at a desk and type into a chatbot. Four people at four screens running four separate conversations with four separate AIs, in the same room, not speaking to each other. The agents are collaborating with nobody. The humans are collaborating with nobody.Everyone is doing, in a shared space, the exact solo work they could have done at home, now with an uncomfortable chair and a commute attached.I know this office because I have been there. I’ve worked as a fractional CPO at a variety of startups over the past few years and some of them required everyone in office for collaboration and culture purposes, and what was actually happening was a floor of people at open desks and shared tables, everyone heads-down in their own tasks, earbuds in, which is not collaborative in any way whatsoever.The only real interaction occurred when somebody took a call out in the open and derailed the eight people near them, who were now straining to hear their own thoughts over somebody else’s pitch meeting. The in-person mandate had not created the intended collaboration. All it did was take solo work that people were doing fine at home and made it harder.This is the part of “Office Space” that could have been a documentary. Peter Gibbons didn’t hate his job because the work was hard. He hated the commute, the eight bosses who each wanted the same TPS report, and the open floor where a man could lean over the partition at any moment to ask why he hadn’t used the new cover sheet.The building added nothing to the work and did create a great deal of misery. The movie played it as absurd, but, frankly, a lot of return-to-office plans have adopted that as an operating model.This is not an anecdote the research argues with. Ethan Bernstein and Stephen Turban put sensors on employees before and after a company tore out its walls for an open floor plan, the layout that is supposed to spark all that spontaneous mingling. Face-to-face interaction dropped by about seventy percent.People responded to being shoved together by putting their headphones on and retreating into email and chat. This is the equivalent of throwing a party, forcing everyone to come, and watching them text each other from opposite corners of the room.So if being in office isn’t producing collaboration, what is the mandate for? Yuye Ding and Mark Ma looked at the S&P 500 companies that ordered everyone back and found no improvement in firm value and a measurable drop in how people felt about the job. Their read was blunt. The mandates lined up with managers using the office to reassert control and to have someone to blame, not to get better work.Forget the productivity numbers. The real cost is the people you lose, and you lose the best ones first.Nicholas Bloom and his colleagues ran a real randomized trial, published in Nature, with more than sixteen hundred employees split between five days in and a hybrid schedule. The hybrid group quit about a third less often, with no hit to performance or promotions.Forcing everyone back five days a week does not buy more output. It buys more resignations, and the first ones gone are the people with somewhere else to go.That a pretty big cost for the privilege of watching your agents do the work in a room full of other people watching theirs.The thing is, the people deepest into AI are the ones who most want to be together, and not to sit in silence. Janet Pogue McLaurin and her team at Gensler surveyed more than sixteen thousand workers and found that the heaviest AI users, about a third of everyone, are also the most collaborative, the most connected to their teams, and the most likely to come into the office. They are coming in for each other.These five-day in-office mandates are coming almost entirely from the biggest companies, and, to be fair, that is the one place the evidence says in-person helps. Arpit Gupta, Abhinav Gupta, and Elena Simintzi tracked remote work across thousands of firms and found it cut productivity at established companies by about nine percent, while raising it at startups by about twelve.Big, old organizations genuinely struggle to coordinate when scattered. Small teams thrive, because remote lets them hire the best people anywhere instead of the nearest people around. So the companies swinging the hardest mandates are the ones with a real coordination problem, and they are solving it by forcing the fix on everyone, including the small teams it only slows down.AI takes the entry-level work from below, distance takes the mentoring from above.What the room is actually forFull disclosure. I have run my company fully remote since 2019, before the pandemic made it “cool.” For most of our work, I still think remote is the right answer. It’s not my favorite thing to admit that I have found that the office turns out to be very good at a few specific things, and that those few things are suddenly the only ones that really matter.Once the agents take the production work, the part of the human’s job that remains relevant is to decide what’s worth making, to catch the thing that’s wrong and to teach the person above and below you on the ladder how to see it too.That happens to be the work the research ties to being in a physical place together.Melanie Brucks and Jonathan Levav ran a study putting pairs together either in person or over video and asking them to generate ideas. The in-person pairs came up with meaningfully more, and more creative, ideas. The video pairs were just as good at the next step, picking which idea to run with.Basically, generating creative ideas is helped by sharing a space, and choosing the ones to implement isn’t. This lines up exactly with the split the agents just created. The machine is a fine partner for narrowing and deciding against known options. It is a worse one for the wide-open, slightly stupid, what-if-we-tried part, and that part goes better with a human across the table.There is one finding that gives me pause, because it’s the real cost of how I’ve chosen to work, and it is definitely one AI has made worse.Someone has to learn to do the actual jobs. People learn skills by sitting near other people who already know how, absorbing the small corrections, asking the dumb question out loud instead of filing a formal ticket for it. Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais measured this and found that junior engineers got dramatically more feedback when they sat near senior ones, and lost about a fifth of it when they went remote.Proximity is how the craft gets handed down. Distance quietly starves it.I feel this one personally, because it is the hardest part of running a company the way I do. One of my own designers, still growing in her career, put it this way. “Constructive feedback is how I know I’m improving, and that’s hard to get when you can’t just walk into your boss’s office and ask them to look at something with you. I’m lucky I’m on a small enough team that I feel comfortable reaching out. If I were part of anything larger, I think it would be much harder. Even on bigger client teams, the feedback I get from people outside my everyday group is thin, when I get it at all.”She is right. The ambient coaching that used to just happen in a room, the over-the-shoulder correction, the pulled-aside-after-a-meeting, does not happen on its own when everyone is remote. We made it happen on purpose.We hold a standing thirty-minute check-in every week, time that exists for nothing but the feedback and questions they’d otherwise have had to catch me in a hallway to ask. It is a deliberate, scheduled replacement for a thing that used to happen a bit more naturally. Remote turns the mentoring into something you have to build on purpose, instead of something you can assume.This isn’t just happening at my company, of course. The KPMG American Worker Survey found AI adoption and office mandates rising together, and concluded that managers are now the linchpin for turning in-person time into real mentorship for the people earliest in their careers, the exact thing a crowded floor of people in headphones does not deliver on its own.Now put that next to what the agents are doing. Remember the Stanford finding, that the entry-level jobs are the ones vanishing, because AI is doing the checkable, process-heavy tasks that used to be a junior’s whole first year. Those tasks were how you learned, by doing the boring version a hundred times until you could feel when it was wrong.Anyone who watched Richie spend a week at that fine-dining restaurant on The Bear understands this. They hand him a mountain of forks to polish and nothing else, and he spends days furious about it, a grown man doing the most menial job in the building. Then somewhere in the repetition it clicks, and he comes out the other side understanding the whole craft in a way no shortcut could have taught him.That was the art of apprenticeship. In our world, the agents are polishing the forks now, and the mentor who would have stood over you while you learned lives on a screen, if they’re there at all.The on-ramp to every one of these careers is being pulled up from both ends at once, by the agents from below and by the distance from above, and almost nobody is talking about the two as the same problem. They are the same problem.This is where the office earns its keep now, if it earns it anywhere. It’s not necessarily a place to produce deliverables, the agents clearly have that, but as the one place a person can still learn the judgment the agents can’t, from another person.You cannot apprentice over a screen share nearly as well as you can over a shoulder.Designers have already championed this work-style. Patrick Neeman has written that the next decade of design work is about owning the systems and the trade-offs underneath the screens, the part you can’t hand to a model. Vlad Derdeicea pointed out that most of a design lead’s day was never mired in pixels in the first place, but rather focusing on aligning, deciding, and convincing. Pushing pixels was a small piece of the day that a machine can now take, which gives leaders more time to do the teaching, which was always the actual job.None of this adds up to an argument for the five-day in-office mandate. It adds up to something narrower. The office matters now for exactly the things it was never really designed to optimize, the idea you’d never have had alone, the greener team member who evolves by watching you work, the trust that only seems to set when people share a space. It matters more than ever, and for less than ever.About a third of American companies now mandate full-time office, the thing the data keeps arguing against.So what is the commute forEvery one of these mandates comes with the same justification. Andy Jassy wrote in his Amazon memo that collaborating, brainstorming, and inventing are simpler and more effective in person, and that teaching and learning from one another are more seamless. Jamie Dimon called the benefits of being together substantial and irreplaceable.The reality is, these leaders are not wrong that those things matter, but it’s worth considering whether they are wrong that a mandate delivers them.Chris Wardman describes this contradiction pretty bluntly, saying companies deploy AI that strips out the everyday interactions where knowledge actually transfers, then mandate attendance to protect the very thing they are automating away.The Flex Index, which tracks the policies of roughly nine thousand companies, now puts about a third of American firms on full-time in-office, and the biggest companies are leading the charge. What that mostly creates, though, is a building full of people doing exactly the work that no longer needs a building. In the meantime, the collaboration they said they wanted is just sitting right there on the mandate, impossible to order up.You cannot schedule serendipity for 9 a.m. Nobody mentors the new kid on command.A good idea has never once shown up because a policy required it. Drag everyone in and chain them to the desks, and all you have manufactured is a more expensive version of the thing they were already doing at home, plus traffic.A move that actually fits the current environment is narrower and a little strange. Treat the office the way you’d treat any specialized tool. You don’t run your whole life out of the one drawer with the good scissors, you open that drawer when you need the thing that’s in there.Nicholas Bloom’s data keeps pointing at the same sweet spot, a couple of deliberate days together, the rest wherever the work actually gets done, which buys the retention and the output without the resentment.Yuan Yuan and his colleagues found the same thing when looking at badge data from forty-three thousand people across a global company’s offices. Left alone, people coordinate their own in-person days around the work and the teammates that actually need to be there.Any mandate that just counts heads on a Tuesday misses the point of being together. Come in for the ideation, the teaching, the arguing, the trust that only seems to set face to face. Then go home and let the agents run the production from a server farm that never needed to see your face anyway.While the office technically never died, it shouldn’t be roaring back to what it was. AI merely changed what it’s for. For a hundred years it was where the work happened and now the work happens in the cloud, and the building is left holding the handful of human things we were always a little embarrassed to admit were the actual point.Ryan Anderson, writing in Forbes about Atlassian’s internal findings, argues that as AI absorbs the routine work, value creation migrates toward the things that require human insight and collaboration, which makes the physical workplace more important, not less. Sure, AI doesn’t need an office, but the people using it do, mainly for the handful of things this quickly moving technology cannot do for them.This brings us back to Alexa’s question. People are coming back to the office, but that was never really the question. The question is what they think they’re coming back to do. If the answer is to sit at a desk and quietly prompt a machine that works fine without them, next to other people doing the same, then they didn’t come back for the right reasons.If people are merely driving in to be alone together, then, that, you really can do from home.References and further readingThe work left the buildingErik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen, “Canaries in the Coal Mine? item.title: What is a researcher’s worth?
item.description: Why the debate over research isn’t a technology story – and why effortless AI makes human friction our scarcest asset.Image created by author, with Midjourney.We’re no stranger to this question.For many years, research practitioners have talked with one another about how to “mature” teams so that they understand the value of our work in bringing success to their ventures. Or when we share the results of our research, we are peppered with questions about whether the findings are real, whether the methods are too weak or lack representativeness, or whether our subjects are even telling the truth when they express to us what they need.But it’s not just research practitioners. Researchers in academia have been stripped of the funding they need to advance science. Academic departments have shuttered, and scholars’ voices have been dismissed as part of major civic scientific efforts, like the Census, the Environmental Protection Agency, or the Department of Education.Put in this context, contemporary discourse around artificial intelligence replacing our jobs feels less like “the reason” than one reason among many when people question whether researchers (and research, in general) matter.Over the last ten years, I’ve worked as an industry researcher while keeping a foot in academia, and have had some of the best work experiences of my life. There is a joy and a magic I find in what happens when you bring experts of different disciplines together – research, business, engineering, design, and more – to solve complex puzzles.So if that cross-disciplinary magic is so real — and so productive — why do researchers in both companies and public life spend so much of their careers on the defensive? Most hot takes right now answer that question with new kinds of work: prompt faster, automate your synthesis, prove your return on investment.As a social scientist, I think those takes miss what is actually happening. The debate over a researcher’s worth isn’t really a technology story. It’s a story about how institutions handle inconvenient truths.Why institutions put research on trial.Back in 2020, I wrote about one of my favorite scenes from the all-too-accurate show, Silicon Valley. In the episode, technologists watch through a one-way mirror as focus group participants give honest feedback about their app. One participant explained that the app made them feel “totally freaked out,” and another explained that it “made me feel stupid.”Behind the mirror, the exec got angry. “Clearly none of these people get it, maybe this is a bad group…everyone that I showed the beta to loved it.” His colleague explained that this was the fifth focus group and they all shared the same feedback. She then realized he only gave the beta to his engineer friends. “I wanted to give it to people who would understand what I’m trying to do so I could get useful feedback,” he said. “And with all due respect, I gave it to you — the one person without a computing background – and you said it felt engineered.”Focus group scene from Silicon Valley (S3E9).Those of us who love the craft of research love talking about research methods. But I find that in many cases, debates about methods in settings like these are not about finding what’s valuable. Methodological nitpicking is a way to avoid disruptions to a preferred plan. In this way, it is a shield against uncertainty – ironically, the very thing that research tries to disambiguate.Social scientists argue that when under pressure, organizations gravitate toward commensuration – a process by which people working together flatten a messy, pluralistic set of realities into a single spreadsheet metric. The truth is, we do live in a world with a lot of unknowns, and the “winners” of today’s marketplace may not be the same in a few months or years. Under that uncertainty, it is tempting to flatten complex human behavior into click metrics – and flatten researchers into headcount cost compared against a chatbot – mistaking a tidy spreadsheet for certainty.What AI actually changed: a mirror that rarely talks back.In 2020, the lead technologist in Silicon Valley had to walk through the door and argue with human beings using their products. In 2026, they don’t have to do that anymore. They can swap the humans behind the glass for a synthetic AI persona trained to give feedback in specific ways.I’m not here to say that AI is bad for science. I actually love a lot of the applications of artificial intelligence I get to use. I’m more troubled by the discourse around artificial intelligence and research in industry – how people talk about it – and the way it is compared to the human worth of social scientists.For one, when organizations treat research as theater to rubber-stamp decisions they have already made, synthetic users and LLM summaries offer “good enough” reassurance at a fraction of the cost. Replacing hard-to-reach or marginalized communities with LLM agents doesn’t actually include them, either. It builds statistical caricatures out of dominant internet texts while erasing human consent and real-world inequities – the kind of blind spot that lets an automated camera “touch-up” feature quietly lighten darker skin tones if real people aren’t in the room.And think about how culture actually moves. A few years ago, if you asked a model trained on historical averages what romance audiences wanted, it would tell you to center a man and a woman falling in love – it never would have bet on a breakout love story about two men playing hockey. Models fed past averages and synthetic data lose the tails of the distribution, the emerging subcultures and edge cases where the future actually starts. Meanwhile, algorithmic platforms mistake digital traces for human intent: a frustrated user clicking three times to fix a broken output looks like “high engagement” in behavioral logs.Models trained on historical averages capture polite consensus in the middle while losing the tails where new culture and real-world blind spots actually start. Diagram by the author, using Gemini.Artificial intelligence is an interesting tool, not a good social scientist. But today, AI is giving anxious institutions the frictionless validation they secretly always wanted.Looking in our own mirror.Listen, I don’t think researchers are perfect by any means. We’re human after all! I actually think that researchers both in industry and academia accidentally made our worth easy to caricature.Often professions survive or shrink based on what they claim jurisdiction over – what we diagnose problems to be, to what we attribute their causes, and how we offer treatment. In 2020, I warned that industry research was used too tactically (“go run a focus group”) as a way to drive impact. But over the last decade, much of industry research leaned into method gatekeeping – measuring our worth by how many people we interviewed or surveyed, or how many “insights” we delivered, or how many slide decks were shared.At the same time, in academia, career incentives rewarded the world’s smartest experts for speaking mainly to peers behind journal paywalls rather than embedding social science into civic and institutional design. For example, a senior professor in my field asked me how I’d like the discipline to advance. I said that we should consider hiring clinical professors to more genuinely bring our findings to the field. He actually laughed at me. “Save it for social work,” he said.I’m of the opinion that neither of these approaches has really helped anyone. In the former, we have traded using appropriate and defensible methods, asking big questions, and discussing complicated answers for a “study complete” checkbox. In the latter, we have siloed the magic of expert discovery almost entirely to the few people who read a published paper.Where the magic of research lives.Why does bringing research, engineering, design, and business together feel like magic? David Stark showed that breakthrough innovation happens in what he calls “heterarchies” – teams that hold competing accounts of worth in creative tension rather than collapsing everything into shipping speed. When AI coding tools let teams spin up twenty working prototypes in a week, velocity is no longer the scarce resource. Knowing which human dream is worth building becomes the scarcest asset in the room. For example, when do you pause a team buried in fifty usability bug fixes to instead ask whether we’re focused on the right value?Some unfortunate news for my colleagues: humans don’t follow linear product models. They improvise inside their own social groups and cultural ecosystems. They react and adapt to major changes in their lives.Engineers see systems; product managers see markets and funnels; and social scientists see social structure.What social structure actually looks like underneath platform metrics: tight-knit intimate pockets, central moderators and bridges holding the wider ecosystem together, and emerging subcultures taking shape at the edges. Diagram by the author, using Gemini.Social scientists can find and explain why youth culture over the last twenty years has shifted from public broadcasting to more intimate pockets of the internet. Or why a certain design aesthetic feels exciting in one region and troubling in another, shaped by the cultural meanings people there share. Or how chaotic-looking livestreams with tens of thousands of people are actually held together by the patterned, organized activities of moderators who keep conversation focused and fun.In The Tacit Dimension, Hungarian-British polymath Michael Polanyi wrote that “we can know more than we can tell.” A vast amount of human knowledge is nonverbal. It includes how we think about cultural norms that we can’t summarize in a survey, or sometimes even in the context of an interview. My bet is that unguided LLMs can’t uncover that tacit knowledge on their own. But social scientists can. We triangulate methods and hold magnifying glasses up to a social problem in a variety of ways, including by testing our assumptions against an accumulated body of scholarly work in purposefully specific subfields.Worth is built together.Whether in a product sprint, a university lab, or a public agency, a researcher’s worth was never the focus group they run, how big or small their sample size is, or the paper they publish. Our worth is how we apply our training and our lens to the messy, plural, inconvenient realities of human life, even when institutions are tempted by easy mirrors that boil experience down to a lone metric.To my research peers: bring your expertise and critical thinking to the work that you do. Show value to your teams by how you and your work “make the strange familiar, and the familiar strange” in the pursuit of a shared understanding grounded in human experience.To my academic colleagues: get out of the ivory tower. Meet people who do research and engage in practice for purposes that have nothing to do with publishing. Learn new ways to talk about your work that shed both academic-ese and didactic habits in favor of two-way learning.To my partners in research: resist the seduction of a mirror that always agrees with you. When AI makes spinning up twenty new ideas effortless, speed stops being your competitive edge – knowing what is actually true about people outside your building is. Invite the friction of someone trained to tell you when your favorite plan doesn’t match how humans really live.We’ve spent years talking about how to “mature” organizations into valuing research, as if worth were a favor. It isn’t. Worth is built together.Dr. Matt Rafalow is a senior staff researcher at YouTube, and a visiting scholar at University of Southern California. The views expressed in this article reflects the individual opinions of the author.What is a researcher’s worth? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: UI edge cases: A reference guide
item.description: A practical reference guide for catching UI edge cases before they ship — organized by category, with how to test, how to detect them in the wild, and how to design a fix. With examples.UI edge cases: A reference guide, a banner image.IntroductionOne day my colleague and I were at a workshop in a client’s office about agentic workflows in UI Design and Development when suddenly the client asked us a very good question.“If we, designers and developers, are left to check the AI’s code for all the small but important edge cases it might miss — why don’t we give a document or a list of UI edge cases to the AI to begin with?”Indeed a very good question, so my colleague and I tasked ourselves with finding a document like this so we could send it to our client.But we couldn’t find anything that was generic enough to fit every client and specific enough to include all the little cases we saw everyday. Between us we have more than 15 years of UI Design and Development background.We did find a few documents that had some of the information we needed as well as some that were industry-specific like documents for the Military, Governments, Medical or Telecom.In the end I was tasked with writing a comprehensive document and sending it to the client for approval and it did end up giving the agentic workflow better results in terms of code generation.So in the name of sharing, I give here the full document paraphrased in human language with some of the more technical code left out to keep it as generic and readable as possible.1. Content-DrivenEmpty statesThis can happen when there’s no data to show yet, zero search results, empty inbox, empty list — screen looks broken or unfinished with no explanation.To test, load the page with a brand-new account or a filtered view that returns nothing, or manually clear a list’s data source.The solution is to design and implement a dedicated empty state — icon / illustration, one-line explanation, a clear next action (e.g., “No projects yet — Create one”).No results for my search. Source: X.Text length extremesLong names or titles that break the layout (overflow, wrapping into other elements), very short or single-character values might look off-balance.We can use pseudo-localization or seed test data with a deliberately long string (e.g., “Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious International Holdings LLC”) and a 1 or 2 character string in every text field, like “I” or “OK”.We can solve this by defining truncation rules per component (single-line ellipsis vs. multi-line clamp vs. wrap) and set max-widths.Text length issues, notice how they use ellipsis everywhere. Source: GitHub.Long unbroken stringsURLs, emails, or IDs don’t wrap, causing horizontal overflow or breaking the container. A user might paste a long URL or a 40+ character token into any field that renders user content.We should decide whether to truncate mid-string (common for hashes / emails) with an ellipsis in the middle, or just allow wrapping.Notice those middle truncations. Source: Mempool.Pluralization and zero countsWordings like “1 items” or “0 item” can read as broken or unpolished. Some languages have more plural forms than English (Russian, Arabic).Force counts of 0, 1, 2, and a large number through any relevant component, test with a locale that has more complex plural rules if you plan to localize.To solve this we need to explicitly copy-write the 0, 1, and many states rather than assuming one template covers all of them. On the development side, we can use an i18n library with proper pluralization.Notice the “1 point / 2 points” and also the “discuss” (no comments) / “1 comment” / “15 comments”. Source: Hacker News.Localization / i18nTranslated text can run up to 40% longer (German, Finnish) or even run shorter, breaking fixed-width buttons and labels. RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew) often need mirrored layouts while dates, numbers and currency formats vary.We can pseudo-localize the UI (wrap strings with padding characters) to simulate expansion using a toggle with dir=”rtl” and browse the whole flow, try switching OS and browser locale when possible.Design components with flexible widths, not fixed pixel widths for text containers, RTL “mirrored” variants for directional icons (arrows, chevrons and more) and “mirrored” interactions if relevant.On the development side use logical CSS properties (margin-inline-start instead of margin-left) so RTL can be flipped automatically.RTL language website (in Hebrew), notice how everything is flipped. Source: Wikipedia.Missing mediaBroken image links, users with no avatar, videos that failed to load — leaves a broken-image icon or an unintended blank space.You can point an src at a 404 URL (an address you know that doesn’t exist) to test this. Also test a user record with a null avatar field, a throttled network to successfully fail media loads.Design a fallback state — initials-based avatar when image fails to load, or a generic placeholder image, a poster frame for a failed video.Missing images — notice the broken-image icons, achieved by throttling the network in dev tools. Source: Wikipedia.2. State-DrivenLoading statesA blank screen or jarring pop-in while data loads — unclear if the app is frozen or if loading takes too long.We can throttle network to “Slow 3G” in devtools and artificially delay API responses in a staging environment.Design skeleton screens that match final content’s shape (not just generic spinners) for anything that takes >300ms and define a timeout state (“This is taking longer than usual”).Loading is taking long, notice the skeleton screen. Source: Twitch TV.Error statesNetwork failures, validation errors, or partial failures (some data loaded, some didn’t) show up as a blank screen, console-only error, or generic “Something went wrong.”Kill the network mid-request, mock a 500 / 403 / timeout response, simulate a request where only some of several parallel calls fail.We should design distinct states per error type (network vs. permission vs. validation) with actionable recovery (a retry button, send bug report etc).Validation error, the page does exist but you’re not logged in so you can’t see it. Source: GitHub.Interim / optimistic statesThe gap between user action and server confirmation is either invisible (user might be unsure if it worked) or the UI update is later reverted, thus confusing the user.We can add artificial latency and watch what the UI displays between click and response, we can force the server call to fail after an optimistic update to see the rollback behavior. Review any “like / save / delete” style interaction.Define a clear pending visual, such as: subtle dimming, spinner on a specific element (not the whole page) and a clear rollback / error treatment if it fails / succeeds.Pending states on buttons. Source: MUI.Permission / auth statesLogged-out views, session expiring mid-action, or insufficient permissions leads to silent failures or confusing redirects.We can expire a session token manually and attempt an action, log in as a lower-permission role and attempt a restricted action, test deep-linking to a protected page while logged out.Design a “session expired” interstitial that preserves the user’s in-progress work where possible, also design disabled / hidden variants for restricted actions with an explanation on hover or on tap.A permission issue. Source: Wikipedia.Stale dataUser might leave a tab open for hours, underlying data changes (deleted by someone else or otherwise updated elsewhere) and the UI still reflects the older state, leading to conflicting edits.To test this — try to open the same record in two sessions, edit in one, then act on the other without refreshing.We should design a “this has changed” banner with a refresh or merge actions rather than silently overwriting the tab, which can be jarring.Stale data banner presented to the end user. Source: Python org.3. Input-DrivenFocus statesKeyboard-only users can’t tell what’s in focus. Focus can get trapped or lost when opening / closing modals or menus.Try unplugging the mouse and navigate the entire flow with Tab / Shift+Tab / Enter / Space / Escape only.Design a visible, high-contrast focus ring as a first-class state for every interactive element (don’t rely on browser defaults, but don’t remove it completely either).Focus states, notice how they’re not the browser defaults. Source: GOV.UK.Disabled / readonly variationsDisabled and readonly states might look identical, or aren’t visually distinguishable enough from enabled states, this can confuse users about why they can’t interact with some elements.Try Placing a disabled, readonly, and enabled version of the same component side by side, or next to a simliar looking component, and see if a new user can tell them apart without any documentation (for example a primary disabled button next to an enabled secondary button).Give the disabled and readonly states a distinct, documented visual treatment (for example: disabled = grayed + no cursor change. Readonly = normal color + lock icon).Input fields in different states, notice how read-only look. Source: MUI.Rapid / repeated inputUsers might double-click a submit button and it shouldn’t fire duplicate requests (double charge, duplicate record, etc.), spamming a button or rapid resize / scroll causes jank or race conditions.Try rapidly double-click and triple-click every button, hold down a resize handle and drag erratically, scroll-flick a long list repeatedly.Show an immediate disabled / loading / read-only state on the button or input field the instant it was clicked.A button that change its state to “loading” when clicked. Source: Loading.io.Copy-pasteA pasted text can carry unexpected formatting, emojis, or control characters that break layout, validation, or storage.Try to copy rich text from a Word doc or a webpage and paste it into every text input or text area. Paste emoji-heavy text and right-to-left text. Paste a string with null bytes or control characters.Decide whether inputs even should accept formatting (a rich text field) or strip it (a plain text field) and be consistent per field type or style.4. Layout / ResponsiveExtreme viewport sizesVery narrow screens (folded phones, for example) or very wide monitors (ultrawide, 3440px+) can break layouts designed for a “typical” resolution range.Resize the browser window to its minimum and to full ultrawide width, you can use devtools device emulation for specific devices or screen sizes.Design with min-width / max-width content in mind, don’t let a single-column layout stretch to a full-width column on an ultrawide display. Don’t let content collapse below a usable minimum either.Extreme small-width display, notice the centered content isn’t centered anymore. Source: Apple.Zoom levelsTry zoom the browser to 200% or use OS text-scaling to break the layout, this can create overlapping texts and cut-off buttons.Zoom browser to 200% (a WCAG requirement) and navigate the full flow. Increase or decrease OS-level text size setting.Design with relative units in mind so text scaling doesn’t require pixel-perfect fixed layouts, otherwise near-sighted users may be unable to use your website.Same website at 100% and 200%, notice how no element stays small. Source: GitHub.Dynamic content changing dimensionsA component resizing based on content (for example: an accordion, a comment with a long reply) can push neighboring elements around unexpectedly, causing a layout shift.Try to trigger the resize (expand accordion, load async content, change dynamic content) and watch for neighboring elements jumping, you can also check Lighthouse’s Cumulative Layout Shift score.To accomodate this, please reserve space or use smooth height transitions rather than instant jumps. Consider whether the expanding element should overlay instead of pushing the content.Expanding accordions example. Source: GOV.UK.Nested scroll containersScroll-within-scroll creates ambiguous scroll targeting (users might scroll the page when they meant scrolling the inner panel, or vice versa).Sticky elements can overlap or conflict, horizontally-scrollable components (carousels, tables) nested in a vertically-scrolling page can hijack diagonal trackpad / touch gestures, or unintentionally introduce page-level horizontal scrolling if content overflows without being contained.We can scroll with our cursor at the boundary between inner and outer scrolling areas. We can test using a trackpad, a mouse wheel, and touch input separately (they can behave differently).Also check for an unexpected horizontal scrollbar on the page itself by resizing the viewport narrower than the widest nested element.Minimize nested scroll where possible. If necessary, give the inner scroll area a clear visual boundary so users can know which scroll will be captured. Avoid mixing scroll axes in adjacent / nested regions where possible.Nested scrolls, notice what happens when a user scroll the sidebar to the end. Source: Tailwind.Safe areasTake into consideration notches, browser chrome, and virtual keyboards covering content or inputs, especially on mobile.Test on an actual notched device (or simulator) in both orientations, also focus a text input near the bottom of the screen and check if the keyboard covers it or shifting the view to reveal it.Try to keep critical content and actions out of the extreme edges. Design for a keyboard-visible state on forms when possible.The importance of testing on a real device. Source: WebKit.5. System / EnvironmentDark mode / forced-colors / high contrastCustom-styled components (checkboxes, radio buttons, focus rings) lose their custom styling or become invisible in forced-colors / high-contrast modes. Dark mode might reveal hardcoded colors that don’t adapt.Toggle OS-level dark mode and Windows High Contrast Mode. Test with devtools prefers-color-scheme: dark / light.Define a full dark-mode palette (not just an inverted light mode) and verify contrast ratios in both modes.A dark-mode made with custom colors. Source: GitHub Docs.Reduced motion preferenceSome users have stated preference for reduced motion and they still get full animations, which can cause discomfort or eye strain.Try to enable “Reduce Motion” in OS accessibility settings and revisit all animated interactions in your site, does it still animate or do you see a fallback instead?We should design a reduced-motion variant for key animations like cross-fading instead of slides and zooms, or instant state changes instead of complex movement.AirPods Pro 3 animation, default on the left and reduced motion on the right. Source: Apple.Font-loading flash (FOUT / FOIT)FOUT is the Flash of unstyled text and FOIT is the Flash of invisible text, both can happen while custom web fonts load, often times with a layout shift when the font swaps.Throttle your network in devtools and reload the page. Compare fallback font metrics to the final font. Lighthouse flags font-display issues and layout shift from font swap.We can try and choose a fallback font with similar x-height / width to the custom font to minimize the layout shift, or we can choose to hide the text itself until the font loads.Same website before the font loads and after. Source: GOV.UK.Offline / flaky connectivityWhen a user is on a flaky network, the app might appear frozen or throws unhandled errors when the network drops or is intermittent.Please use the devtools to simulate “Offline” mid-session. Use a network-throttling proxy to simulate packet loss or a flaky connection.Design an offline banner / indicator and, if feasible, an offline-capable mode (view cached data, queue actions, local host etc).YouTube’s “offline mode”, to be fair it can still play downloaded videos. Source: YouTube.Closing thoughtsI hope this list can be the bare-minimum standard of UI edge cases that are checked and taken care of, from localization to error states to offline mode, there’s no reason to leave them out anymore.Next year I’m sure we’ll have more edge cases that will pop up once those are already fixed, I have high hopes for this industry that with the emergence of AI the standard for good software will only get higher.If this list made you, or your AI, spit out more usable code or a better thought out product overall, please share this article online.Thanks for reading, and I’d love to hear your experience in the comments, also if I missed any edge cases — please tell me and I’ll roll it into the next version of this article.SourcesApple Human Interface Guidelines — PatternsThinking like a developer, part II: design the edge casesEdge Cases in UX/UI ExplainedUX Edge CasesDesigning for Edge Cases: UX That Works When Things Go Wrong20 Edge Case Examples in Software That Product Teams MissUI edge cases: A reference guide was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
